props.title: Sympathy for Mr. Vengeance
props.initialSlug: Deaf man's organ deal spirals into brutal revenge cycle

sections.content: Sympathy for Mr. Vengeance launches Park Chan-wook's Vengeance Trilogy with raw, unflinching brutality. The film follows a deaf factory worker's desperate attempt to secure a kidney transplant for his sister, spiraling into a devastating chain of violence. Unlike the more stylized Oldboy (2003) or the darkly elegant Lady Vengeance (2005), this film strips revenge down to its bare, ugly essence. Park's surgical direction forces us to confront the futility of retribution through long takes, minimal dialogue, and green-tinted cinematography that makes even daylight scenes feel sick with dread.

sections.content: The film's influence resonates through modern Korean revenge cinema, establishing themes that directors like Kim Jee-woon would later explore in I Saw the Devil (2010). Where Japanese revenge films like Lady Snowblood (1973) often embrace stylized violence, Park Chan-wook creates a world of moral ambiguity where every act of vengeance breeds only more suffering. The film's industrial settings and focus on class warfare would later influence works like Parasite (2019), showing how economic desperation breeds violence.

What sets Sympathy for Mr. Vengeance apart is its radical empathy for both victim and perpetrator. Unlike the righteous revenge of Kill Bill Vol. 1 (2003) or the cathartic violence of The Man from Nowhere (2010), Park forces us to understand and feel for every character caught in the cycle of violence. The use of Song Kang-ho as a grieving father seeking revenge creates a complex mirror to Shin Ha-kyun's desperate brother, making both men's actions simultaneously understandable and horrific. sections.content: Park's unflinching exploration of violence influenced a generation of filmmakers. Drive (2011) borrowed its neon-tinged brutality, while Blue Ruin (2013) echoed its focus on the messy, unglamorous nature of revenge. The film's emphasis on sound design - particularly in scenes featuring the deaf protagonist - created a template for sensory-focused thriller elements later seen in films like A Quiet Place (2018).
